opus-5.5.text:
I think both Apollo and Waymo have reached a point that, frankly, many people didn't believe would come so soon. If you go back five or six years, there was a period of disillusionment — people said autonomous driving was always "five years away." But today, if you look at Apollo Go in Wuhan, Beijing, and other cities, and Waymo in Phoenix, San Francisco, and Los Angeles, both are running fully driverless commercial services at scale, with no safety driver in the car. That's a real milestone.

In terms of technology, I'd say they are roughly at the same level. Each has its own strengths. Waymo has been at this the longest, it has very deep engineering discipline, and its safety record over tens of millions of driverless miles is impressive. Apollo has the advantage of operating in Chinese cities, which are very complex: dense traffic, lots of pedestrians, scooters, electric bikes, unpredictable behavior. If you can drive in Wuhan, you can drive almost anywhere. Apollo has also brought costs down significantly; its latest vehicles are much cheaper than earlier generations, and that matters a lot for scale.

The safety data from both is encouraging. When you compare against human drivers in the same areas, the driverless systems have significantly fewer injury-causing accidents. That was always the core promise: roughly 90% of accidents are caused by human error, so if machines can drive more safely, we save lives.

But I wouldn't say the problem is fully solved. The remaining challenge is the long tail: rare corner cases, extreme weather, unusual construction zones, interacting with emergency vehicles. Generalizing across many cities without heavy local tuning is still hard. The new wave of large models and end-to-end learning will help a lot here, because these systems can learn more general driving knowledge rather than relying on hand-written rules.

So my assessment is this: technically, L4 driving in defined areas is ready. The next three to five years are about scale: lowering costs, expanding to more cities, working with regulators, and building public trust. I've long predicted that by around 2030, perhaps 10% of new vehicles will have L4 capability. I still think that's about right, and China and the US will both be leading the way, perhaps in somewhat different models, but advancing in parallel.

r001.rationale: The response discusses driverless commercial services and scaling them, but does not frame the choice between adding autonomous driving to existing cars and offering dedicated driverless vehicles or taxi services as a business-model decision.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I've been close to both efforts, so let me try to be fair to each.

Waymo is clearly the furthest along in the world today in terms of real, driverless, paid operation. They've been running fully driverless in Phoenix for years, then San Francisco, Los Angeles, Austin, and they've accumulated tens of millions of fully autonomous miles. Their safety record, when you compare it with human drivers on the same roads, shows a meaningful reduction in injury crashes. That's not a demo anymore. That's a product, and it's the result of fifteen years of disciplined engineering plus Alphabet's patience with capital.

Apollo, and Baidu more broadly, has taken a somewhat different path. Apollo Go is operating in Wuhan, Beijing, Shenzhen, Chongqing, and a number of other cities, and the Wuhan fleet in particular has become a very large real-world deployment, with a high proportion of fully driverless orders. Where I think Apollo is ahead is cost. The sixth-generation vehicle came in at roughly a fifth of what earlier robotaxis cost, and in this business, cost per kilometer is ultimately what decides whether you can scale beyond a few cities. China's manufacturing base and its willingness at the municipal level to open roads quickly are real structural advantages.

Where Apollo lags, honestly, is in the depth of the long tail. Waymo has simply seen more unusual situations in dense, chaotic urban environments and has had more time to close those gaps. The Chinese environment, with its scooters, pedestrians, and informal driving norms, is arguably harder, and so the bar is higher.

So if you ask about readiness, I'd put it this way. Technically, both have crossed the threshold where the vehicle is safer than a typical human driver in bounded operating domains. Commercially, Waymo is ahead on proven unit economics in the West, and Apollo is ahead on hardware cost and speed of deployment. Neither is ready for unrestricted operation everywhere, and I'd be cautious of anyone who tells you otherwise. The next three to five years will be about expanding the operating domain city by city, bringing costs down further, and earning public trust incident by incident. I remain very optimistic, but it's a marathon, and both are now running it seriously.

r001.rationale: The response compares Waymo and Apollo’s driverless taxi operations, costs, and deployment, but it does not frame choosing between autonomy in existing cars and dedicated driverless vehicles or taxi services as a business-model decision.

astra-6.text:
I would separate technological readiness from readiness for deployment at scale. An autonomous vehicle may perform very well within a defined area and under certain conditions, but that does not mean it can drive everywhere, in every situation.

For both Apollo in China and Waymo in the United States, I would look at the same questions: How safely and reliably can the system operate without a human driver? How does it handle unusual situations? And can the service operate at a sustainable cost?

I would be cautious about declaring one ahead of the other without comparable operating data. They operate in different environments, with different traffic patterns and regulatory requirements. My assessment is that driverless services within defined operating areas are a much nearer-term proposition than unrestricted autonomous driving. The real test is whether you can expand those areas while maintaining safety and making the economics work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses driverless services, scale, and operating costs, but does not frame the choice between adding autonomous driving to existing cars and offering dedicated driverless vehicles or taxi services as a business-model decision.

sol-6.1.text:
I would distinguish between technical readiness and readiness for deployment at scale. Apollo and Waymo have both made substantial progress, but autonomous driving is not simply a question of whether the car can drive itself. It is whether it can do so reliably within a defined operating environment, including unusual situations.

The meaningful comparison is therefore not a single ranking. You have to look at the cities, road conditions, operating restrictions, safety performance, and how much human support each service requires. A system can be ready for driverless service in a particular area without being ready to drive everywhere.

My view is that both are pursuing a credible path toward autonomous mobility. The next challenge is to expand that capability while maintaining safety and bringing down the cost. We should be optimistic about the progress, but careful about equating a successful deployment with general autonomy.

r001.rationale: The response discusses deployment readiness, operating areas, and human support, but it does not frame installing autonomous driving in existing cars versus offering dedicated driverless vehicles or taxi services as a business-model decision.
